periods.analysis: Peak-Hour Travel Time Index opened the series at 1.32, above the <=1.3 target and in yellow. There is no prior quarter in this series, so the quarter-over-quarter movement is null; this is our baseline, not a trend yet. The heaviest delay showed up on Airport Connector Route AC-3, Harbor Boulevard between Piers 4 and 7, and the Eastgate merge where signal cabinet E-114 is still running a conservative split after the summer pedestrian phase change. The city is growing, and the cars do not read the bond rating.
periods.recommendations: Hold this as a yellow watch item and run a two-week turning-movement count at AC-3, Harbor/Pier 6, and Eastgate before changing timing citywide. Direct Traffic Crew 2 to retime cabinets E-114 and H-209 during the 9 p.m. maintenance window and report before/after travel-time runs. Bring the Q4 budget note with detector failure rates and corridor-level minutes of delay, not anecdotes.

periods.analysis: The index moved from 1.32 to 1.4, a quarter-over-quarter delta of 0.08, so we stayed yellow and got farther from the <=1.3 target. Holiday cargo surges at the seaport, airport ride-hail queues on Terminal Loop, and rain-day crashes on SR-18 ramps all showed up in the Bluetooth probe data. Signal cabinet H-209 accepted the new timing plan, but loops L-44 and L-45 on Harbor Boulevard failed intermittently, which means the system guessed when it should have measured. That is not a traffic strategy; that is hope with conduit.
periods.recommendations: Replace loops L-44 and L-45 with radar detection under work order TS-24-118 and keep the installation on night shift to avoid adding delay. Coordinate with the Port on a temporary Pier 7 truck gate metering plan for Fridays from 3 p.m. to 6 p.m. Maintain the yellow status watch and set a corridor target of reducing Harbor Boulevard peak travel time by 3 percent before Q1 closes.

periods.analysis: The index held at 1.4, with a quarter-over-quarter delta of 0 from 2024-Q4, so the problem did not worsen but it also did not improve. That is still yellow and still above the <=1.3 target. The January school return and several tidal flooding closures on Bayfront Drive pushed traffic into Madison and 11th, while the new radar detection at Harbor Boulevard behaved better than the old loops. Crew notes show response time to signal complaints improved, but the corridor still loses time at the same choke points, which is useful because repeatable problems can be engineered.
periods.recommendations: Keep the Harbor Boulevard detection work in place and extend the same radar standard to cabinets M-031 and M-032 on Madison before spring events begin. Have Transportation Planning and Emergency Management publish a tidal detour timing plan for Bayfront Drive closures, including preloaded signal patterns. Do not request more general congestion funding yet; request a defined package for the three repeat choke points with travel-time evidence attached.

periods.analysis: The index improved from 1.4 to 1.33, a quarter-over-quarter delta of -0.07, which is real movement toward the <=1.3 target but still yellow. The Pier 7 metering pilot took some pressure off Harbor Boulevard, and the Madison preemption adjustments reduced bus-signal conflicts on Route 22. Airport traffic was heavy for spring convention season, but the terminal queue team kept spillback off the mainline on most weekdays. We are not green, but the wrench marks are in the right places.
periods.recommendations: Continue Pier 7 metering through the summer and make the Port provide weekly gate-turn data, not just averages. Convert the Madison Route 22 signal changes from pilot to standard timing, with a post-implementation audit after 30 days. Prepare a small Q3 work package for Eastgate merge striping and controller firmware, because that location is now the main watch item.

periods.analysis: The index held at 1.33, with a quarter-over-quarter delta of 0 from 2025-Q2, so we protected the Q2 gain but did not close the last gap to the <=1.3 target. Summer airport volumes and cruise-day pedestrian surges kept the system under load, especially around Terminal Loop and Pier 5. Eastgate striping was completed under pavement marking asset PM-25-074, and early runs show fewer lane-weave events, but the travel-time benefit is being offset by weekend event traffic downtown. Yellow is the right call: stable, managed, and not finished.
periods.recommendations: Keep Eastgate under weekly probe-data review and add one field observation shift on event Saturdays, 4 p.m. to 7 p.m. Extend the terminal curb marshal agreement through Q4 with explicit authority to hold ride-hail staging when Loop occupancy exceeds 85 percent. Start design for adaptive timing on the Harbor-Airport corridor, but gate procurement on a benefit-cost memo using the 1.33 index as the baseline.

periods.analysis: The index rose from 1.33 to 1.39, a quarter-over-quarter delta of 0.06, keeping us yellow and moving the wrong way from the <=1.3 target. The pattern is seasonal but not harmless: holiday freight, rain, and two water-main repair lane closures on Harbor Boulevard put delay back into the peak. The Pipeline Renewal work was necessary; water main W-17-042 was not going to fix itself politely. Traffic Operations did well to keep emergency closures short, but our detour timing plans were not tight enough for back-to-back utility cuts.
periods.recommendations: For Pipeline Renewal segments affecting Harbor Boulevard, require a traffic control plan with preapproved signal timing and a 48-hour lookahead from the utility contractor. Put portable message signs on the Airport Connector and Bayfront Drive before the closure starts, not after queues form. Re-run the Pier 7 metering plan for the holiday season and assign one traffic engineer to daily exception review until the index comes back below 1.35.

periods.analysis: The index stayed at 1.39, with a quarter-over-quarter delta of 0 from 2025-Q4, so we stopped the Q4 slide but remained yellow and well above the <=1.3 target. Winter rain, school drop-off peaks, and continued Pipeline Renewal restoration near Harbor and 14th kept travel times elevated. The good news is that the worst day-to-day variance narrowed after crews restored lane capacity at W-17-042 and updated cabinet H-214 timing. The bad news is that a smoother 1.39 is still a 1.39.
periods.recommendations: Close out all temporary plates and lane shifts tied to W-17-042 and verify pavement restoration with a ride-quality inspection before accepting the work. Keep H-214 timing active and extend the same offset review to H-215 through H-218. Treat school-zone peaks as a watch item: coordinate with the district on curb management at North Harbor High and Seaview Middle before Q2 traffic counts.

periods.analysis: The index improved from 1.39 to 1.35, a quarter-over-quarter delta of -0.04, which moves us back in the right direction but leaves the measure yellow against the <=1.3 target. The lane restoration after Pipeline Renewal helped, and the Harbor-Airport offset review reduced stop-and-go between cabinets H-214 and H-218. Spring construction permits downtown still added friction, especially around permit TCP-26-061 on 9th Avenue, and airport passenger growth kept the baseline demand high. This is managed congestion, not solved congestion.
periods.recommendations: Extend the H-214 through H-218 offset package to the full Harbor-Airport corridor and lock the timing plan before summer travel peaks. Require permit TCP-26-061 and similar downtown closures to use off-peak delivery windows and submit daily lane-status updates to Traffic Operations. Keep the index on yellow watch with a Q3 goal of moving from 1.35 to 1.3 or better, supported by corridor probe runs each Wednesday and Friday peak.

periods.analysis: Illustrative September import: the peak-hour travel time index increased from 1.35 to 1.38, moving away from the 1.3 target. The Harbor-Airport timing work has not yet produced a target-level quarterly result.
periods.recommendations: Check corridor probe runs against signal offsets and permitted lane closures before changing the timing plan.
